newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's trade unions drift toward open defiance.
newsitem.headline: Canada's trade unions drift toward open defiance.

text.p: While Canada's central bank Gov. Gordon Thiessen gave an upbeat report to a parliamentary finance committee, labour leaders promised Canadians more work stoppages, protests and general economic mayhem.
The contrast between Thiessen's rosy economic projections and labour's apocalyptic warnings were the clearest indication yet of the widening chasm between capital and labour in Canada.
This year has seen record bank profits, soaring stock markets and plunging interest rates. The dormant Canadian dollar made a comeback. Canadians even started believing economists.
At the same time, Canada has witnessed bitter labour unrest not seen since the early 1980s.

The toll included a prolonged autoworker's strike, an illegal teachers walkout and a series of city-wide shutdowns culminating last month in a massive day of protest that virtually shut down the country's largest city, Toronto.
The fruits of this labour, or lack thereof, are apparent.

Ontario, Canada's most industrialised and populous province, suffered four times as many days lost through work stoppages this year than 1995, according to a report released this week by the Ontario Federation of Labour (OFL).
Union leaders offer no apologies for steering their membership on a collision course with deficit-slashing provincial governments.

"We, in the labour movement, will not shy away from confrontation and strife, from pickets and strikes to defend ourselves, our families, our rights," Ontario Federation of Labour President Gordon Wilson said in a statement this week.
"I expect the number of work hours lost due to strikes will skyrocket in the next couple of years," Wilson predicted.
Trade union bravado is by no means exclusive to Ontario.

In neighbouring Quebec, leaders of the main unions have taken separatist Premier Lucien Bouchard to the woodshed over a proposed deficit-reduction plan that would cut wages and benefits in the public sector.
Six unions representing the mainly French-speaking province's 400,000 public sector employees want their members to vote in favour of a massive strike that could paralyse the Quebec government.

The call to arms is a break with the usually sympathetic attitude of Quebec labour toward pro-sovereignty governments. This time, however, the unions say they are not going to take a bullet for Bouchard.
"The government has left us no other choice but to play hardball," said Lorraine Page, president of the province's main teachers' union.
Labour's drift to open defiance is oddly out of synch with an overall decline in the strength of the Canadian trade union movement.

Union membership in Canada -- currently pegged at 33.9 percent of the non-agricultural paid workforce -- has gradually declined since 1978. That trend is expected to continue as Canada makes the jump from a smokestack economy to one more reliant on technology and light industry.
Companies with 20 or fewer employees are responsible for 85 percent of all new jobs created in the new Canadian economy, according to some estimates.
"The smaller firms are becoming more important, and they tend to operate in non-union settings," said David Brown, senior policy analyst with the Canadian Chamber of Commerce.
He said Canada was falling into line with the United States where unions cover a thin layer of the private-sector workforce.
"The union movement in Canada is going to become more of a public-sector animal," Brown predicted.
Ironically, it is this strength in the public sector which may prove labour's greatest weakness.

Governments throughout the land -- from the neo-conservative Ontario Tories to the quasi-socialist New Democrats of British Columbia -- are stripping the civil service bare in a desperate attempt to cut costs.
The resulting avalanche of pink slips, combined with wage cuts and "restrictive" labour laws, has brought the trade union movement full circle to its infant days as a legion of street fighters.
That is an image that has been doggedly courted in this year of discontent, and it is one that union leaders say is here to stay.
